touches.text: The abstract ticket owns what every kind shares: its birth (cast) and its three parts, each with one job: the plan (only what a builder builds from), the metadata and state (what gates and doors read and write as it moves), and the history (the append-only log). WHY: one job per part reduces confusion; a builder reads the plan and nothing else.

The workflow drives it. When a step's work is finished, the ticket asks that step's gate. Once the gate passes, its post-gate probes send mail over the bus to every device that can do the next step, naming the step (BUILDME, PROVEME, ...), and a device comes to claim it. A builder never goes looking for what's next: it gets the mail and does that. When several compete, the least capable one that thinks it can do it claims it, "leaving the more capable in case a bigger one comes along."

The miss. A walk that cannot leave the top, or scores under the floor everywhere, cannot answer. Then, and only then, the LLM is asked, given the question, the string, and the tree's vocabulary at the node where it stopped: which of these answer it, or what new node belongs under this one? It returns names, existing or new, and nothing else, so the integration is plain code: a new node goes in the one list and under its parent; the string's words are added to the named nodes' counts. Then the walk runs again and lands. That is the learning: the next string like it needs no LLM.

One bus per cairn instance, not per host. Each box runs its own bus, and the buses talk to one another, so a device always talks to the bus on its own box; together they are the instance's one bus. A device runs on one box; the other boxes reach it over the buses. No box needs a full set of devices. WHY: so the instance can run several heavy tasks at once across boxes.

An instance is declared by its folder existing in class-space: cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/ (one address in two roots). Declared = the folders (read by the rack tool, 17.20); running = which of those are in the rack.
She is NOT a builder: Claude and aider build. She owns the care of the code: the inspectors, gates, processes and workflows the builders pass through are hers to own and, eventually, to optimize.

Prebuild face: the chart chain, eight machines, each answering one question before a build begins: orient (what is asked, where does it live), constrain (what bounds it), survey (what already exists), decompose (how does it split), triage (what first, by what standard), hypothesize (what do we expect, how would we know we're wrong), validate (what does DONE mean, measured), and after the build, verdict (what done actually meant).

Watcher face: watches the code and the builders' work over time, reasons over it with graph trees (held by the librarian's delegation), and learns the failure modes. Learns from: code, chat logs, books, past projects, CC's failure modes.

The chart chain machines (9.3.2): orient, constrain, survey, decompose, triage, hypothesize, validate, verdict. [Q#98: The verdict's instrument run, and the proofs that exercise it, need bubblewrap, which Windows does not have, so `cairn test --exec` refuses there ("the instance seal is not confirmed ... bubblewrap (bwrap) is not installed") and three teeth stay red on Windows: test_the_instrument_is_run (two teeth) and the standing-verdict-proofs-stay-green check. Measured 2026-11-13. Whether Windows gets its own seal is the per-OS seal question in Q#90 (9.4.2.3.3); this one is the narrow choice that stands beside it: until that is settled, do the bwrap teeth skip on Windows (and read as not-run there), or do they stay red until Windows has a seal of its own?]

Skills (skills/: cairnhelp, challenge, chart, commit, intent, sorted, ...) are Claude Code's. The deterministic parts move out of markdown into CC device verbs: a skill's OS-side work runs as a script, and CC's shim processes the result and injects it into the session. WHY: every habit captured that way is one CC no longer spends inference on, so CC gets faster; a first charting pass done in deterministic Python with no LLM until after saved about 90% of tokens, measured in real use.
feedback: where a component's failing findings go (the -2-> edge). WHY: a finding that goes nowhere teaches nothing. USERS: the inspectors.

metric: records a measurement of anything. WHY: a metric is a primitive; its job is to measure whatever it is, and like feedback (which a metric strictly is) it must eventually have a consumer. USERS: any probe or tool.
